summary:
SPACE LARP Inc has developed the Lunar Landing Site Navigator: an interactive tool for exploring candidate lunar landing sites, with a focus on the south pole. Its 3D lunar globe, searchable site list, and site panels let mission planners, educators, and the public move quickly between locations and dates. For each selected site and time, users can review solar-power estimates, energy charts, terrain, and Sun/Earth visibility. The immersive "Lunarium" view places users at the site, showing the Sun and Earth against NASA-derived terrain, with controls to scrub or play through time and inspect given time windows.

This matters because small changes in date or location near the lunar poles can affect solar power and direct-to-Earth communications. The tool brings those planning factors into one accessible visual experience.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator (live at https://lunarsky.select) is a web tool for rapidly evaluating lunar landing sites.

What it does and how it works:

Pick a site and a date. The tool shows where the Sun and Earth sit in the local sky, time to sunrise and sunset, solar power available (W/m² and daily kWh/m²), and when direct-to-Earth communication is possible. It has three views:

  • Landing Sites: a 3D globe built from real NASA imagery, with a side panel per site showing location, terrain, slope, roughness, live power and a 30-day timeline.
  • Lunarium: stand at a site in first person and watch the Sun and Earth move across the real terrain horizon. On a phone it uses the motion sensors, so you can point your phone around to look.
  • Playground: enter any coordinates, click "Calculate potential", and get site info, a 2D terrain map and power results, with the option to add the site to the catalogue.

A FastAPI backend queries JPL Horizons for the Sun's position at each site and turns it into power per m² and sunrise/sunset times. The frontend processes NASA LOLA elevation data in the browser: global data at about 1.9 km per pixel, and 5 m per pixel at key south-polar sites. From it, the frontend builds terrain and works out where the horizon is in every direction from the site.

Benefits and intended impact

At the south pole the Sun skims the horizon, and Earth bobs above and below it. A crater rim or a few days' slip can make a site unusable. Existing tools (Quickmap, Moon Trek, Horizons) are powerful but built for deep analysis, not quick comparison. Our tool turns this into a few seconds of point-and-click. The aim is to help mission planners, including teams on NASA's commercial lander program (CLPS), students and even astronauts, re-check sites and dates quickly when schedules change. Because each view's state is kept in its URL, a view can be shared with a link.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, three.js, Recharts, JavaScript.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, astroquery (JPL Horizons), NumPy, Pydantic.
  • Data: NASA LRO LROC imagery, LOLA elevation (CGI Moon Kit) and PGDA 5 m polar terrain.
  • Hosting: Netlify (frontend) and Render (backend).

No special hardware is needed. Lunarium also works on phones.

What makes it creative

  • Lunarium turns numbers into an experience. You don't read "Sun 1.2° above horizon"; you stand on Shackleton's rim and watch it graze the ridge.
  • Mission-control interface. The UI is designed to feel like a real operations console.
  • Real terrain, not a smooth sphere. Terrain is sampled on a local flat grid around each site, so it stays accurate even at the pole.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy where it matters: terrain horizons at the pole, and handling coordinates near ±90°.
  • Honesty about data: anything still modelled is labelled in the UI. Earth's position and visibility come from a simplified model until the backend supplies them.
  • Team workflow: a single data layer and a documented data contract, so the UI and Python work could proceed in parallel.
  • Speed and accessibility: quick comparisons, shareable links, mobile support, and charts that don't rely on colour alone.
